extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, philosophers of mathematics, math educators, and students of mathematical practice
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging and producing mathematical proofs from a Lakatosian perspective: proofs as dialectical, history-laden processes that evolve via conjectures, counterexamples, lemma revision, and concept change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as a thought-experiment / living dialectical process
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'proof' in living mathematics is not a formal derivation in a calculus but a thought-experiment that decomposes a conjecture into sub-conjectures (lemmas), invites criticism of any lemma, and improves the theorem statement, the lemmas, and the underlying concepts in response to counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat formal textbook proofs as fossils; emphasize the dialectical history (attempts, failures, counterexamples) that led to the final result. Present work so others can replay and critique the discovery process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose conjectures into explicit lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Break conjectures into sub-conjectures (lemmas) rather than relying on a single monolithic argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the structure of the argument explicit so individual lemmas can be inspected, criticized, and revised if counterexamples appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose lemmas individually; avoid hidden lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: A good proof exposes its lemmas individually so they can be challenged; hidden or 'obvious' steps that conceal essential content are a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a step appears 'obvious', state it as a lemma and justify it; hidden lemmas are anti-patterns because they prevent proper critical scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim simultaneously to prove and to refute (Rule 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a conjecture, set out both to prove it and to refute it — inspect lemmas and possible counterexamples in the same field of vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively search for counterexamples while attempting proofs; treating proof and refutation as twin activities improves robustness and exposes weaknesses early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish and respond to global counterexamples (Rule 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a global counterexample (satisfies the hypothesis but not the conclusion) is found, identify the 'guilty lemma' and either reject it or qualify the theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace which lemma the counterexample defeats, then decide whether to strengthen hypotheses, drop the lemma, or alter the statement so the conclusion becomes valid again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish and respond to local counterexamples (Rule 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a local counterexample (breaks one lemma) is found, check whether it is also global; if not, refine proof analysis and the decomposition into lemmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local counterexamples to improve the proof structure; determine whether the flaw is in an isolated lemma or in the overall argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma-incorporation / revise theorem by promoting lemmas to hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite the theorem to exclude counterexamples by promoting the offending lemma (or condition) to an explicit hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that theorem statements may be legitimately qualified in light of counterexamples; record such revisions transparently as part of the proof history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept-stretching is a legitimate corrective move
rubrics_metrics.description: Use counterexamples to stretch or revise the definitions of concepts (e.g., 'polyhedron') so that the theorem survives in a deeper form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual revision is not cheating; it can lead to more fruitful and general theories. Document how and why a concept is stretched and show that the stretched concept is fruitful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples to deepen the theorem (Rule 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a counterexample of any type, try to use it to stretch the concept or revise the argument so the theorem survives in a stronger or more illuminating form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View counterexamples as opportunities for conceptual and theoretical improvement rather than merely obstacles to be dismissed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monster-handling reflects mathematical taste: monster-adjusting over monster-barring
rubrics_metrics.description: When awkward or 'monster' cases arise, treat them honestly (monster-adjusting) by modifying concepts or proofs rather than excluding them by definitional fiat (monster-barring).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monster-adjusting can reveal deeper structure; monster-barring hides problems and is discouraged. How a community treats monsters reveals its methodological virtues or vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem should be the strongest consistent with the proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer a theorem statement that is the strongest statement consistent with the proof rather than pre-emptively weakened versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid weakening statements unnecessarily to make proofs easier; seek maximal results that the evidence supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge dialectical history in presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Good mathematical work acknowledges the dialectical history — prior weaker forms, counterexamples, and monster-cases — instead of presenting only a polished final derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the sequence of conjectures, refutations, lemma revisions, and conceptual changes when possible; this transparency helps future critique and development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Euclidean/deductivist presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present proofs as if they sprang fully formed and hide the discovery process; this 'Euclidean' style obscures the real epistemic work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor transparent exposition of failed attempts, counterexamples considered, and the reasoning that led to the final form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid definitional dogmatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusing to revise definitions in the face of counterexamples is an anti-pattern; definitions should be open to revision to improve theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to alter foundational definitions when justified by examples and conceptual payoffs; document reasons for any definitional changes.
